No individual speaker is named in this line. The formula is a narrative frame introducing a sequence of individual dream reports (in the fuller 4Q530 columns the reports are then delivered by named giants). The speaker is not named in the surviving portion of the line; the phrase באראכאל אבוי הוה עמי ('Barakel my father was with me') identifies the speaker's father as Barakel. 3. 4Q531 1:6 — אוהיא (Ohya) is the speaker, in direct speech introduced by באדין אמר אוהיא לה ('then Ohya said to him'). The addressee is the third-person singular suffix לה, whose identity depends on the preceding column (in the fuller 4Q531 sequence the interlocutor is Mahway). Ohya's role here is dreamer-narrator; the phrase אנס עלי חלם ('a dream has been forced upon me') presents the dream as an imposition from outside the dreamer's will — a theologically loaded idiom, not merely "I had a dream."

(b) COMMON FORMULA FOR DREAM NARRATION

The shared syntactic skeleton across the three witnesses is:

  [temporal/discourse marker] + אמר/ואשתעיו + [dreamer] + [audience] + חלמא/חלום + [report]

Element-by-element:

- Narrative introduction of a report: ואשתעיו חלמיהון (4Q530) — plural, with the object חלמיהון ('their dreams') expressed.
- Introduction of direct speech: ואמר לאוהיא ... אחי (6Q8) — singular, with the dream content following in the first person.
- Introduction of direct speech with explicit dream-object: אמר אוהיא לה אנס עלי חלם (4Q531) — the dream is grammatically foregrounded as the topic.

The invariant core is therefore the verb אמר/שתעי governing a dream-object (חלם/חלום/חלמיהון), with the dreamer in the subject position and the audience marked by a prepositional or pronominal complement. The formula is not identical across witnesses; it is a family of related formulas. I will not claim a single Ur-form.

Note the lexical variation: Aramaic חלמא/חלום (cf. Biblical Aramaic חֶלְמָא) versus the plural חלמיהון. Do not normalize these.
